gap_proposals.description: The runbook states the backend pushes a speed cap within two seconds of pedestrian-zone entry, but July 2026 telemetry shows a median 11-second delay to cap acknowledgement, a slowest decile exceeding 40 seconds, and 6,914 of 41,206 entries with no recorded cap command. Both observations are preserved; no visible authority resolves them.

The stated intent requires confirming that a ride cannot be ended outside the service area, but none of the supplied sources describe software behavior, code, tests, telemetry, or runbook rules for that requirement.

Available telemetry concerns speed-cap commands and acknowledgement delay, not measured scooter speed inside pedestrian zones. There is no visible evidence that scooters actually slowed to walking pace, including after acknowledgement or when no command was recorded.

The permit language requires slowing to walking pace, while the runbook specifies a 6 km/h cap. Visible material does not say whether 6 km/h is the permit definition, a city-accepted equivalent, or an internal choice.

Telemetry reports entries with no speed-cap command, and the dispatcher discards low-accuracy updates without recording them. Those facts permit materially different readings: no command issued, command issued but unrecorded, or a mix. The 6,914 figure cannot be attributed on the visible material.

The former contractor's account that the 15-metre accuracy filter was added after city complaints about capping outside the zone is presented without a decision record, permit correspondence, or ticket in the handed-over material.

Code shows a 15-metre accuracy gate, and a former contractor offers an uncorroborated reason for it. No visible authority, decision record, or permit correspondence resolves whether that filter is required, permitted, or in conflict with the walking-pace rule.

The desired outcome is confirmation that software actually enforces both permit rules before renewal review, but no measurable success condition is given (for example required cap coverage, latency, actual speed, or ride-end rejection rate).

Dispatcher tests only use 5-metre accuracy updates and do not cover discarded low-accuracy updates or never-capped scooters. Discarded updates are also not recorded, so missed caps cannot be proven or tested from the described telemetry path.
No test, telemetry, code path, or runbook check is supplied that would prove a ride cannot be ended outside the service area.

Visible telemetry of frequent missing and late caps, unrecorded discarded position updates, absent actual-speed evidence, and no evidence for the service-area end-ride rule leave permit-renewal confirmation uncontrolled. No compensating control is described.
The runbook source is dated 2025-04 while the telemetry window is July 2026. Treating the runbook as a description of current enforcement depends on evidence that may no longer be current.

Runbook, telemetry, dispatcher code, and tests together are not sufficient to justify a conclusion that software enforces walking pace in pedestrian zones. The visible measurements concern command issuance and acknowledgement, show large miss and delay rates, and omit actual speed.

It is unclear what counts as software enforcement: backend cap commands only, scooter firmware behavior if a command is missing or late, cap release on zone exit, or on-device speed control. Hardware/firmware is frozen, but the software boundary that must be confirmed is not specified.

Cap issuance depends on receiving a position update with accuracy radius below 15 metres. Low-accuracy updates are discarded without retry or record, so enforcement depends on GPS quality that is known and unresolved in the supplied material.

The bounded source set contains no code, tests, telemetry, or operational document about ending rides outside the service area, so the requested confirmation of that permit rule cannot be reasoned from the supplied context.
The runbook states the speed cap is released only when the scooter leaves the pedestrian zone, but no telemetry, tests, or code about cap release are supplied.

semantic_proposals.mission: Confirm that existing fleet software enforces both city-permit rules—slowing to walking pace inside marked pedestrian zones, and preventing a ride from being ended outside the service area—before the permit renewal review, without changing hardware.

semantic_proposals.statement: Confirm that software actually enforces slowing scooters to walking pace inside marked pedestrian zones.
Confirm that software actually prevents a ride from being ended outside the service area.
Produce a confirmation, suitable for the permit renewal review, that both permit rules are enforced by software on the current fleet.
Scooters must slow to walking pace inside marked pedestrian zones.
A ride cannot be ended outside the service area.
Hardware must not be changed; every scooter in the fleet is the same model and firmware line.
Changing scooter hardware or moving the fleet off the current firmware line is out of scope.
The operator runs two thousand three hundred e-scooters under a city permit.

The operations runbook states that when a scooter enters a pedestrian zone the backend pushes a 6 km/h speed cap to the scooter within two seconds, and that the cap is released only when the scooter leaves the zone.

Telemetry for July 2026 covering 41,206 pedestrian-zone entries shows 6,914 entries with no recorded speed-cap command; among entries that did receive a command, median delay from zone entry to cap acknowledgement was 11 seconds, and the slowest decile exceeded 40 seconds.

The geofence dispatcher issues a cap command only when it receives a position update whose reported accuracy radius is below 15 metres; updates with a larger accuracy radius are discarded without retry and without being recorded anywhere.

A former contractor stated by email that the 15-metre accuracy filter was added because the city complained about scooters being capped on the pavement outside the zone; no decision record, permit correspondence, or ticket supporting that account is present in the handed-over material.
The dispatcher test suite exercises only position updates with a reported accuracy radius of 5 metres and does not cover a discarded low-accuracy update or a scooter that never receives a cap.
The runbook 6 km/h speed cap is the intended software implementation of the permit's walking-pace rule.
Entries that recorded no speed-cap command are cases where no cap was issued, rather than issued commands missing from telemetry.
Backend-pushed speed-cap commands on the current firmware are sufficient, without hardware change, for the software to enforce walking pace inside pedestrian zones.

semantic_proposals.prompt: How, if at all, does the current software prevent a ride from being ended outside the service area?
Does the city permit define walking pace as 6 km/h, or is 6 km/h only an internal runbook choice?
What measurable condition would count as confirming that software actually enforces both permit rules for the renewal review?

semantic_proposals.question: Whether and how software currently enforces that a ride cannot be ended outside the service area.
Whether scooters actually reduce speed to walking pace after a cap command, including when no cap command is recorded.
